items.prompt: Which knife grip is the standard safe way to hold a chef's knife while chopping?

options.label: Pinch the blade just above the handle with thumb and forefinger
Grip the end of the handle with the blade pointing sideways
Hold only the handle with all four fingers and the thumb on top
Rest the index finger along the spine with the thumb underneath

rubric: The pinch grip gives the most control and safety.
Handle-only grips are common among beginners but give less control.

items.prompt: What is the term for cutting food into small, even cubes of about 0.5 cm?

options.label: Chiffonade
Julienne
Brunoise
Batonnet

rubric: Brunoise is a very fine dice.
Julienne is matchsticks, chiffonade is ribbons of leaves, batonnet is thick sticks.

items.prompt: At what temperature, in °C, does water boil at sea level?
rubric: Water boils at 100°C at sea level.
Other values are common guesses without basis.

items.prompt: What is the safe minimum internal temperature, in °C, for cooked chicken?
rubric: Poultry is considered safe at 74°C (165°F).
Lower values are for items like medium-rare beef.

items.prompt: Which cooking method uses a small amount of fat in a hot pan and quick cooking of small pieces?

options.label: Steaming
Braising
Poaching
Sautéing

rubric: Sautéing means quick cooking in a little fat over fairly high heat.
Braising and poaching use liquid, steaming uses vapor.

items.prompt: Which of the following are basic tastes that cooks balance when seasoning? Select all that apply.

options.label: Sour
Umami
Crunchy
Salty
Spicy-hot

rubric: Salty, sour and umami are recognized basic tastes.
Crunchy is texture and chili heat is a pain sensation, not a basic taste.

items.prompt: Maya is starting a recipe that says 'dice the onion, then sauté it until translucent.' She has never cooked before and wants to know what 'translucent' means before she starts.

options.label: The onion pieces turn soft and see-through without browning
The onion pieces turn firm and pale yellow, with dry, hardened edges
The onion pieces stay white and opaque, with all their moisture sealed in
The onion pieces turn deep brown and crisp at the edges, with a sweet smell

rubric: Translucent means softened and glossy, with little or no browning.
Brown and crisp describes caramelized or burnt onion.

items.prompt: Why should you pat meat dry before searing it in a hot pan?

options.label: Dry meat absorbs salt better, and the salt makes it brown faster
Water on the meat makes the pan hotter, so the outside burns
Surface moisture must evaporate first, which delays browning
Dry meat cooks more slowly, so the center stays juicy inside

rubric: Moisture steams the surface and prevents browning.
Distractors invent effects of dryness on salt and temperature.

items.prompt: Why do cooks usually add salt to the water when boiling pasta?

options.label: It makes the water boil much faster than plain water
It seasons the pasta as it absorbs the cooking water
It keeps the pasta from sticking by forming a thin film on it
It stops the pasta from absorbing any of the water

rubric: Salted water seasons pasta from within.
Salt does not meaningfully speed boiling or stop water absorption.

items.prompt: Which best explains why vegetables for roasting should be cut into similar-sized pieces?

options.label: Similar pieces cook at a lower oven temperature than uneven ones do
Similar pieces need less salt because they are the same size
Similar pieces absorb oil faster because they have equal surface area
Similar pieces brown evenly because they finish cooking together

rubric: Even size gives even doneness.
Other options misattribute oil, salt or temperature effects.

items.prompt: A recipe says to 'preheat the oven to 200°C.' What is the main reason for this step?

options.label: Food starts cooking at the right temperature, so timing and browning work
Food dries out less when the oven is already hot before it goes in, since it spends less time inside
The recipe time is counted only after the oven has cooled slightly from its peak, so the food does not scorch
The oven needs to burn off food residue from earlier use before it can safely cook anything new

rubric: Preheating makes the recipe's timing reliable.
Other options are myths about residue or cooling.

items.prompt: Which situation is an example of cross-contamination?

options.label: Storing cooked rice in a sealed container in the fridge
Using one board for raw chicken, then salad, unwashed
Cooking chicken until the thickest part reaches a safe temperature
Washing hands with soap before touching any ingredients

rubric: Raw meat germs spread to ready-to-eat food on shared surfaces.
The other options are safe practices.

items.prompt: Which statements correctly explain why a dull knife is more dangerous than a sharp one? Select all that apply.

options.label: It bends the food away from the blade, which makes it easier to hold
It crushes food, which makes the pieces slide on the board
It cuts deeper because it is heavier
It gives less control over where the cut goes
It needs more force, so it is more likely to slip

rubric: Dull blades need extra force, slip and give poor control.
Dullness doesn't add weight or make food easier to hold.

items.prompt: Sam is sautéing mushrooms. He puts a whole pound into a small pan at once, and they end up pale and watery instead of browned. His friend suggests a change for next time.

options.label: Cover the pan with a lid so the trapped steam can brown the surface
Add more water to the pan so the mushrooms cook evenly all over
Turn the heat down so the released water has time to soak back in
Cook in smaller batches so moisture can evaporate and they brown

rubric: Crowding traps steam, so cooking in batches lets moisture escape.
Lids and added water increase steaming and block browning.

items.prompt: Why should you pat a steak dry with paper towels before searing it in a hot pan?

options.label: Paper towels remove bacteria, so the steak can safely cook at lower heat
Surface moisture must boil off first, so a wet steak steams and browns poorly
Dry meat absorbs salt faster, which is what creates the brown crust
Water on the meat lowers the fat content, so the crust turns out tough

rubric: Browning needs a dry surface above water's boiling point; moisture causes steaming.
Distractors confuse drying with salting or food safety.

items.prompt: Why is a roasted chicken usually left to rest for 10 to 15 minutes before carving?

options.label: Resting cools the skin so it turns crisper once it is carved
Juices settle back into the meat, so less runs out when you cut
Resting finishes killing bacteria that survived in the oven
Resting lets the meat shrink so slices come out thinner and neater

rubric: Resting lets juices redistribute and thicken, so the meat stays moist.
Distractors give plausible but wrong effects such as safety or crispness.

items.prompt: Why do most recipes tell you to salt the water generously when boiling pasta?

options.label: Salt firms up the pasta's surface, so it holds its texture and cannot overcook
Pasta absorbs water as it cooks, so salt seasons it throughout
Salt raises the water's temperature, so it boils faster and the pasta cooks sooner
Salt coats the pasta strands as they cook, so they do not stick together

rubric: Pasta absorbs the cooking water, so salted water seasons it from inside.
Distractors repeat common myths about boiling speed, sticking and texture.

items.prompt: Which of these is a dry-heat cooking method?

options.label: Simmering
Steaming
Poaching
Roasting

rubric: Roasting uses hot air without added liquid, so it is dry heat.
The others cook with water or steam, which are moist-heat methods.

items.prompt: Why do recipes ask you to cut vegetables into pieces of similar size?

options.label: Smaller pieces absorb more seasoning, so every piece tastes equally salty
Same-size pieces cook at the same rate, so none are raw or mushy
Equal sizes let the pan hold steady heat, so you can skip stirring
Uniform cuts seal in the juices, so the vegetables keep their flavour

rubric: Cooking time depends on piece size, so uniform pieces finish together.
Distractors invent unrelated benefits like flavour or less stirring.

items.prompt: Which signs tell you the oil in a pan is hot enough to start sautéing? Select all that apply.

options.label: The oil shimmers and flows thinly across the pan
A small piece of onion sizzles as soon as it touches the oil
The oil is giving off heavy smoke and has turned dark
The oil is thick, cloudy and barely moves when you tilt the pan
Faint ripples appear on the oil surface

rubric: Shimmer, ripples and an immediate sizzle show the oil is at sautéing temperature.
Heavy smoke means the oil is overheated, and thick, cloudy oil is still cold.

items.prompt: A home cook piles a full pound of sliced mushrooms into a small skillet over medium-high heat. After a few minutes the mushrooms are grey and sitting in liquid instead of turning golden. What best explains this?

options.label: The pan was too hot, so the mushroom surfaces seized up and forced their water out
The mushrooms needed more oil, since a dry pan always pulls the liquid out of them
Mushrooms are too watery to brown in a skillet, so the grey colour is expected
Crowding cooled the pan and trapped steam, so they simmered in their own liquid

rubric: Too much food in the pan cools it and traps moisture, so food steams instead of browning.
Distractors blame heat or oil, or wrongly claim mushrooms cannot brown.

items.prompt: A recipe for 4 servings uses 300 g rice and 600 ml water. You are cooking for 6 using the same ratio. How much rice and water do you need?

options.label: 400 g rice and 800 ml water
600 g rice and 900 ml water
450 g rice and 900 ml water
450 g rice and 600 ml water

rubric: Scale both by 1.5: 450 g rice and 900 ml water.
Distractors scale only one ingredient or use the wrong factor.

items.prompt: You are making roasted vegetables in a hot oven. Which approach is most likely to give browned, tender-crisp results?

options.label: Spread them on a tray with no oil, so the dry surface crisps up as they bake
Boil them first in a pan, then put them in a cold oven to finish
Pile the vegetables deep in a small dish and cover with foil to hold in heat
Toss with oil and salt, then spread in one layer on a large tray

rubric: A single layer with oil gives dry, even contact with heat so the vegetables brown.
Covering or crowding traps steam, and skipping oil leaves them dry and unevenly cooked.

items.prompt: You have halved an onion from root to tip and peeled it. To dice it with the least effort, what should you do next?

options.label: Cut lengthwise and crosswise, leaving the root end intact, then slice across
Chop straight across the half into thin rings, then cut each stack of rings in half to make pieces
Cut the half into large chunks, then chop the chunks repeatedly until they are the size you want
Cut off the root end first so the layers separate, then mince the onion with a rocking motion

rubric: The intact root holds the layers together while lengthwise and crosswise cuts set the dice size.
Other options give uneven pieces or a less controlled cut.

items.prompt: A recipe calls for 1 tablespoon of dried oregano, but you only have fresh oregano. Roughly how much fresh should you use?

options.label: 1 cup
1 tablespoon
1 teaspoon
3 tablespoons

rubric: Fresh herbs are weaker by weight and volume, so about three times the dried amount is used.
Using the same or less amount would under-season the dish.

items.prompt: You have simmered a vegetable soup for 30 minutes and it tastes flat, though nothing is burnt or sour. What should you do first?

options.label: Boil it hard for ten more minutes to concentrate the flavour
Add a cup of water so the flavours spread out
Add a pinch of salt, stir, and taste again before adding more
Add plenty of black pepper until you can taste the heat

rubric: Flat soup is usually under-salted, so season in small amounts and taste between additions.
Dilution, hard boiling or heavy pepper do not fix a salt deficit.

items.prompt: You are preparing raw chicken and a salad for the same meal. Which actions reduce the risk of cross-contamination? Select all that apply.

options.label: Rinse the raw chicken in the sink to wash germs off
Cut the chicken on a separate board from the one used for salad vegetables
Wipe the board with a dry cloth and reuse it for the salad
Wash your hands with soap after handling the raw chicken
Wash the knife and board in hot soapy water before they touch ready-to-eat foods

rubric: Separate boards, handwashing and proper washing of tools keep raw juices off ready-to-eat food.
Rinsing chicken splashes germs around, and a dry wipe does not clean a board.

items.prompt: A recipe says to roast 1-inch potato cubes at 220°C for 25 minutes. You cut yours into roughly half-inch pieces so they will cook faster. The oven and tray are the same as the recipe's. What is the best way to proceed?

options.label: Cook for the full 25 minutes, since the oven temperature is the same as in the recipe
Start checking at about 12 to 15 minutes, since smaller pieces finish sooner
Lower the oven to 120°C and keep the 25 minutes so the smaller pieces don't burn
Cook for 45 minutes, because smaller pieces need longer to brown and crisp up

rubric: Smaller pieces cook faster, so check early and adjust the time by doneness.
Keeping the full time risks burning, and lengthening it or cutting heat ignores how piece size affects cooking.

items.prompt: A stew for 4 people uses 1 tsp salt. You are making a triple batch for 12 in a large pot. What is the best way to season it?

options.label: Add 4 tsp at the start, since large batches lose salt as they cook
Add about 2 tsp early, then taste near the end and adjust
Add 1 tsp only, since a bigger pot makes salt taste stronger
Add exactly 3 tsp at the start, since salt must scale in step with volume

rubric: Seasoning does not scale linearly in big batches, so start under the full multiple and adjust by tasting.
Distractors treat salt as a fixed ratio or assume it is lost in cooking.

items.prompt: You want to roast potato chunks (about 40 min at 220C) and zucchini slices (about 15 min) on one tray. Which plan gives the best result for both?

options.label: Roast both together and lower the oven to 160C to even out the timing
Shred the zucchini thinly and add it with the potatoes so both brown together
Roast both together under foil so the zucchini steams gently
Roast the potatoes alone first, then add the zucchini for the last 15 minutes

rubric: Items with different cooking times should be staggered so each finishes at once.
Distractors try to force the same timing, which loses browning or overcooks the zucchini.

items.prompt: You need to sear four steaks, but your 10-inch pan holds only two without touching. What should you do?

options.label: Fit all four in and lower the heat so they cook through slowly
Add a splash of water and cover the pan so all four cook evenly
Sear all four in turn on a medium-low flame, so the pan never overheats and the fat doesn't smoke
Sear two at a time in a hot pan, keeping the first pair warm while the second cooks

rubric: Cooking in batches keeps the pan hot and the surface dry so the steaks brown rather than steam.
Distractors crowd the pan or lower the heat, both of which prevent a crust.

items.prompt: A recipe says to finish pasta in the sauce. The package says 10 minutes. Which sequence follows that method?

options.label: Drain at about 8 minutes, discard the water, and add the pasta to the sauce
Cook the full 10 minutes, then simmer 5 more minutes in the sauce to absorb flavour
Drain at about 8 minutes, keep a cup of cooking water, and finish in the sauce
Cook the full 10 minutes, rinse in cold water, then stir it into the sauce

rubric: Undercooking slightly and finishing in sauce with starchy water lets the pasta absorb flavour and bind the sauce.
Distractors overcook the pasta or throw away the starch that helps the sauce cling.

items.prompt: You must dice a whole round carrot into even 1 cm cubes. What is the safest, most effective first step?

options.label: Hold the carrot in your palm and slice toward your hand for speed
Slice straight across into coins, then stack the coins and cut them into cubes
Rock the knife at its tip on the round carrot without steadying it
Trim a thin slice off one side to make a flat, stable base

rubric: A flat base stops the carrot rolling, giving control and even cuts.
Distractors leave the carrot unstable or put the hand in the blade's path.

items.prompt: A recipe for a long-simmered sauce calls for 1 tbsp dried oregano and 1 tsp dried thyme, but you only have fresh herbs. Which adjustments are sensible? Select all that apply.

options.label: Add woody fresh thyme early, since it holds up to long simmering
Dry the fresh herbs in the oven first, since fresh herbs cannot be added raw
Use the same 1 tbsp of fresh oregano, since fresh herbs are stronger
Use roughly three times the volume of fresh oregano

rubric: Fresh herbs are milder by volume, so use more, and woody herbs like thyme tolerate long cooking.
Distractors assume equal amounts or that fresh herbs need drying.

items.prompt: Your recipe roasts a 1.5 kg chicken at 200C for 70 minutes. The bird you bought weighs 2.2 kg. You want it cooked through with moist meat. What is the best approach?

options.label: Roast longer than 70 minutes and check the thigh reaches 74C
Roast at 230C for 70 minutes so the larger bird finishes in the same time as the recipe
Roast 70 minutes, then judge by whether the skin looks golden brown and crisp all over
Multiply the time exactly by 2.2/1.5 and skip any further checks on the meat

rubric: A larger bird needs more time, and internal temperature is the reliable measure of doneness.
Distractors rely on a fixed time, a hotter oven or surface colour.

items.prompt: Roasted broccoli comes out pale and soft, though the oven was at 220C and the florets were oiled. The tray was piled two layers deep. What best explains the result?

options.label: The oven was too hot, so the outsides sealed and the insides steamed in their own skins
Crowded layers trapped moisture, so the florets steamed instead of browning
The oil coating was too thin to conduct heat from the tray into the florets
Salt added before roasting drew out water and softened the florets' texture

rubric: Crowding traps released water vapour, which steams food and blocks browning.
Distractors blame oil, salt or heat, which do not match the symptoms.

items.prompt: A cook adds onions and minced garlic to a hot pan together. After 3 minutes the garlic is dark and bitter while the onions are still raw. What is the underlying cause?

options.label: The garlic was minced too finely, so it released too much sulfur and needed more salt to balance it
The onions released too much water, which cooled the pan and kept the garlic from cooking evenly
The pan was too small, so the garlic could not spread out in the oil and was cooked unevenly
Tiny garlic pieces with little moisture burn much sooner than larger onion pieces at high heat

rubric: Finely minced garlic burns quickly; it should go in after the onions or at lower heat.
Distractors blame onion moisture, pan size or salt rather than differing burn rates.

items.prompt: A vegetable soup has enough salt, but tastes dull and flat. The cook is about to add more salt. Which diagnosis and fix are best?

options.label: It needs more salt, because flat flavour is always under-salting
It needs more water, because dull flavour means the soup is too concentrated
It lacks acidity, so a squeeze of lemon or splash of vinegar should lift it
It lacks sweetness, so a spoonful of sugar will fix the flatness

rubric: When salt is adequate, flatness often signals missing acid, which brightens flavours.
Distractors assume salt, sugar or dilution rather than balance.

items.prompt: A steak, taken straight from its wet packaging and put into a medium-hot pan, turns grey and tough with no crust. Which factor best explains the missing crust?

options.label: Seasoning with salt before cooking pulled out the crust-forming proteins
The steak was too thick, so the outside could not brown at all
Surface moisture and modest heat made it steam before it could brown
Steaks only brown properly if cooked in butter instead of oil

rubric: Moisture on the surface must evaporate before browning begins, so wet meat in a moderate pan steams.
Distractors blame salt, fat type or thickness, which do not explain the grey surface.

items.prompt: Pasta is boiled, then rinsed under cold water and tossed with a tomato sauce. The sauce slides off and pools at the bottom of the bowl. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: The tomato sauce was too acidic to bond with the pasta surface
Rinsing washed off the surface starch that helps sauce cling
The pasta water was not salted enough, so the pasta stayed slick
The pasta was boiled in too much water, so it absorbed too little

rubric: Surface starch helps sauce adhere, and rinsing removes it.
Distractors point to acidity, water volume or salt, which do not affect cling this way.

items.prompt: A roast chicken has dark, nearly burnt skin, yet the meat near the bone is undercooked. Which factors could plausibly explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: Too much salt was rubbed on the skin, which stopped the meat cooking
The bird went into the oven straight from the fridge
The bird was large and thick, so heat reached the centre slowly
The oven temperature was too high for the bird's size
The bird rested too long, which undid the cooking

rubric: Excess surface heat, a cold core and thick meat all make the outside finish before the inside.
Salt does not prevent cooking, and resting happens after cooking.

items.prompt: A cook doubles a beef stew recipe and cooks it in one tall, narrow pot with the lid on, for the original time. The sauce is thin and the beef is still tough. Which diagnosis best explains both problems?

options.label: The beef was cut too small, so it released extra water into the sauce and its fibres tightened up
The doubled salt drew moisture out of the beef, which toughened it and thinned the sauce
The flame was too strong, so the stew boiled hard and broke down its thickener and the meat
The pot has less surface area for evaporation, and the bigger mass needs longer to tenderise

rubric: Doubling in a narrow, covered pot slows evaporation, and a larger mass takes longer to become tender.
Distractors blame salt, heat or cut size, which do not account for both symptoms.

items.prompt: A cook sautés a full pound of sliced mushrooms in a 10-inch skillet over medium-high heat. They turn gray, rubbery and wet instead of golden. Which cause best explains this?

options.label: Mushrooms were salted too late, so the surface never drew out enough water to brown properly
The heat was too high, so the outsides seized and pushed their water inward before browning started
Crowding drops the pan temperature, so released moisture pools and the mushrooms steam instead of browning
The fat was too plentiful, so the slices boiled in oil and could not reach a browning temperature

rubric: Overcrowding cools the pan and traps moisture, so steaming replaces browning.
Distractors blame heat, salt timing or oil quantity, which misread how evaporation gates browning.

items.prompt: A whole roast chicken comes out with dry breast meat, yet the thighs are still slightly pink at the bone when the breast hits its target temperature. What best explains the mismatch?

options.label: The breast's skin is thinner than the thigh's, so it cooks faster, and removing the breast skin before roasting would even out the timing
The thighs sit lower in the oven, so hotter air reaches the breast first and cooks the breast unevenly while the thighs stay cooler
Lean breast is done at a lower temperature, while collagen-rich thighs need higher heat to turn tender
The thighs hold more water, so they absorb oven heat more slowly and always lag behind the breast, whatever the final temperature

rubric: Lean breast and collagen-rich thighs have different ideal finishing temperatures, so one oven time fits only one.
Distractors invent oven-position or skin explanations rather than muscle composition.

items.prompt: A cook's tomato sauce tastes acrid and bitter. The method was: heat oil until shimmering, add minced garlic, stir 2 minutes, then add onions and tomatoes. Which step is the most likely source?

options.label: Cooking minced garlic alone in very hot oil for 2 minutes, which scorched it before other ingredients cooled the pan
Using oil rather than butter, which cannot carry garlic flavor at high heat without turning the whole pan bitter and acrid
Mincing the garlic finely, which releases bitter sulfur compounds even when it is cooked gently at low heat
Adding tomatoes after the onions, which let the onions scorch before any acid could balance their sugars and bitterness

rubric: Fine garlic burns quickly in hot fat with nothing to moderate it.
Distractors blame cut size, ingredient order or fat type, which are not the main burning cause.

items.prompt: A cook boils spaghetti, rinses it under cold water, then tosses it with a hot tomato sauce. The sauce slides off and pools on the plate. Which diagnosis is most accurate?

options.label: The pasta was overcooked, so its swollen, waterlogged surface repelled the sauce once it was drained and cooled
Rinsing washed off the surface starch that helps sauce cling, so nothing holds the sauce to the noodles
The sauce was added too late, so the noodles had already set and their cooled surface would not absorb any liquid
The sauce was too acidic, so its acid broke down the noodle surface and kept it from binding as they cooled

rubric: Surface starch helps sauce adhere; rinsing removes it.
Distractors point to acidity, doneness or timing, which do not explain slipping.

items.prompt: A cook pats a steak lightly, sears it in a heavy pan heated for one minute, and the steak is gray on the outside after four minutes with plenty of liquid in the pan. Which pairing of causes is most likely?

options.label: A damp surface plus an underheated pan, so moisture had to evaporate before browning could start
A pan that held too much heat plus a long sear, which pulled juices out faster than a crust could form
A steak that was cold from the fridge plus a lean cut, which lowered the pan's heat and stopped any crust forming
Too much oil in the pan plus a thick cut, which together shallow-fried the steak and blocked a crust from developing

rubric: Browning needs a dry surface above water's boiling point; surface moisture and weak preheating stall it.
Distractors cite oil, meat quality or pan weight, which are not the main limiting factors.

items.prompt: A tray of cubed carrots and potatoes roasted for 40 minutes comes out pale and soft with no caramelized edges. Which factors could plausibly explain this? Select all that apply.

options.label: The tray was covered with foil, trapping steam
The vegetables were tossed with a little oil beforehand
The vegetables were cut into similar-sized cubes
The pieces were piled several layers deep on the tray
The oven was set to a low temperature of about 150C (300F)

rubric: Trapped steam, crowding and low heat all prevent surface drying and caramelization.
Oil and uniform cuts help roasting, so they do not explain the pale result.

items.prompt: A home cook doubles a beef stew recipe and cooks it in a much larger pot with the same 90-minute simmer and doubled salt and spices. The stew is thin and tastes diluted, though the meat is tender. What is the best explanation?

options.label: Doubled salt and spices dissolved unevenly in the larger volume, so the flavor stayed concentrated at the bottom
The wider pot has less evaporation relative to volume, so less liquid reduced and the flavors stayed dilute
The meat released twice as much liquid, which cannot be offset by a longer simmer
Tender meat always dilutes the broth, so a stew cooked to doneness will taste thinner when scaled up

rubric: Scaling volume does not scale evaporation proportionally, so the stew reduces less in the same time.
Distractors invent dissolving, release or tenderness effects not supported by how reduction works.

items.prompt: A cook wants crisp-skinned chicken thighs in 25 minutes, using one oven-safe skillet and minimal cleanup. Which method best meets those criteria?

options.label: Sear the thighs in a ripping-hot skillet for 3 minutes per side and serve them as soon as they brown
Start skin-side down in a moderately hot skillet to render fat, then flip and finish in a hot oven
Roast the thighs on a covered tray for 25 minutes so the heat cooks them evenly and keeps the skin moist
Boil the thighs for 10 minutes, then pan-fry them in oil until the skin turns golden brown

rubric: Rendering fat skin-side down then oven finishing gives crisp skin and cooked-through meat in one pan.
Distractors add moisture or skip full cooking, which fails the crisp-skin or doneness criteria.

items.prompt: A cook has 45 minutes before searing a thick steak. Criteria: well-seasoned beyond the surface, and a dry exterior for browning. Which salting plan is best?

options.label: Skip salt until after searing, since any earlier salting will dry the meat out
Salt right as it hits the pan, so no moisture is drawn out before searing
Salt generously, leave it uncovered on a rack now, and pat dry before searing
Salt 10 minutes before cooking, which draws out the most surface liquid at the time of searing

rubric: Salting 45 minutes ahead gives time for moisture to draw out and be reabsorbed, leaving a dry surface and seasoning inside.
The 10-minute option leaves wet surface moisture, and the others miss seasoning depth.

items.prompt: A recipe for chicken soup uses 1 tablespoon of fresh thyme and 1 tablespoon of fresh parsley. The cook has only dried herbs and wants to preserve both herbs' character. Which adaptation is best?

options.label: Replace both with dried herbs in equal amounts and simmer them from the start so the flavor fully infuses the broth
Use dried thyme early in about a third of the amount, and add the parsley, or a pinch of dried, only at the end
Leave out both herbs and add extra salt and black pepper, because dried herbs cannot approximate fresh flavor in soup
Replace both with equal amounts of dried herbs and stir them in at the very end so their flavor stays bright and fresh

rubric: Dried herbs are more concentrated and suit early cooking, while delicate parsley flavor fades with long heat.
Distractors ignore concentration or timing differences, or abandon the herbs.

items.prompt: While making dinner, a cook has four hazards. Ranking by likelihood of causing foodborne illness, which is the greatest risk?

options.label: Cooking a burger to 71C (160F) in the center and resting it for two minutes
Slicing raw chicken on a board, then slicing salad tomatoes on the same board without washing it
Storing raw chicken on the bottom shelf of the fridge in a sealed container
Leaving a pot of rice to cool on the counter for one hour before refrigerating it

rubric: Raw poultry contaminating a ready-to-eat food with no kill step is the highest risk.
The other options are either reasonable practice or lower-risk.

items.prompt: A cook wants to brown chicken pieces and then make a pan sauce from the browned bits left behind, while only owning one pan. Which pan is the best choice for those criteria?

options.label: A non-stick skillet, because the bits release easily and can be wiped into the sauce
A thin aluminum saucepan, because it heats quickly and keeps the bits from burning
A deep stockpot, because its high sides keep the fond from burning and let liquid reduce slowly
A stainless steel or cast iron skillet, because it browns well and leaves fond to deglaze

rubric: Stainless or cast iron develops fond that deglazing turns into sauce.
Non-stick limits fond, and thin or deep pots brown poorly.

items.prompt: A recipe says to "sear the roast first to seal in the juices." A cook wants to judge this advice fairly. Which statements are valid evaluations? Select all that apply.

options.label: Searing creates no waterproof barrier, as seared meat still loses moisture while cooking
Searing before or after roasting gives similar flavor, so order can be chosen for convenience
Searing makes the meat retain measurably more juice than not searing
Searing is worthwhile mainly for the browned flavor and texture it adds
Skipping the sear is worse for food safety, as the crust kills internal bacteria

rubric: Searing adds flavor via browning, but it does not seal in juices.
The other claims misstate moisture, safety or equivalence of timing.

items.prompt: A cook is searing pork chops over high heat and wants both a good crust and a rich butter flavor. The cook's first plan is to melt butter in the pan and sear the chops in it. Which revised approach best meets both criteria?

options.label: Sear in oil with a high smoke point, then add butter at the end to baste once the heat is lowered
Sear in oil, then skip the butter, as butter should never be used with any heat above medium
Sear in butter at high heat, then cover the pan so the milk solids can steam rather than burn
Sear in the butter at medium-low heat so it never browns, trading some crust for butter flavor

rubric: Oil handles high heat for crust, and butter added late gives flavor without burning milk solids.
Other options sacrifice crust, risk burning, or reject butter unnecessarily.

items.prompt: You must sear four 3 cm steaks in one 28 cm skillet. Your criteria are deep browning and even doneness across all four. Which approach is best?

options.label: Sear two at a time in a very hot pan, since crowding drops the pan temperature and steam stops browning
Pour in oil to reach halfway up the steaks, since more fat moves heat faster and builds a better crust
Fit all four in at once over medium heat, since lower heat prevents burning and cooks them more evenly
Cover the pan with a lid after flipping, since trapped steam speeds cooking and keeps the crust moist

rubric: Crowding lowers pan temperature and releases moisture, so the meat steams instead of browning; batches keep the pan hot.
Distractors target beliefs that lower heat, lids or extra oil improve browning.

items.prompt: You are roasting a 2 kg chicken and want well-seasoned meat and crisp skin. Judged against both criteria, which salting plan is best?

options.label: Boil the bird briefly in salted water first, since this seasons deeply and makes the skin crisp later
Salt the skin heavily only, since salt crisps the skin and has no need to reach the meat underneath
Salt just before roasting, since salt applied earlier always draws out water and leaves the meat dry
Salt all over and rest uncovered in the fridge overnight, since the surface dries as salt moves inward

rubric: A dry brine lets salt dissolve in surface moisture and be reabsorbed while the uncovered skin dries, serving both criteria.
Distractors reflect the myth that early salting dries meat or that seasoning can stay on the skin.

items.prompt: A cook wants to make a pan sauce from the browned bits left after searing chicken. Judged by how well the pan supports building that sauce, which pan is best?

options.label: A stainless steel skillet, since fond forms on its surface and dissolves when deglazed with liquid
A nonstick skillet on high heat, since the extra heat creates more fond that lifts off easily
A nonstick skillet, since its coating releases food cleanly and leaves the purest sauce base
A thin aluminium foil tray, since it heats quickly and the bits dissolve into any liquid added

rubric: Stainless steel lets fond develop and cling, so deglazing captures that flavor.
Distractors confuse easy release with a better sauce and ignore that nonstick pans develop little fond.

items.prompt: You double a braise (1 tsp salt, 500 ml stock for 1 kg meat) to 2 kg meat in the same covered pot in the oven. Judged by final flavor and texture, which adjustment is best?

options.label: Double the salt and triple the stock, since more meat soaks up extra liquid and seasoning, then skip tasting until serving
Use about 1.5 tsp salt and stock to halfway up the meat, then taste at the end because reduction concentrates salt
Keep the salt and stock unchanged, since the pot size sets how much seasoning and liquid the dish needs, then adjust the oven heat
Double the salt and stock exactly, since ratios must scale linearly for an identical result, and cook for the same time

rubric: Evaporation and liquid needs do not scale linearly, so under-scaling salt and tasting late avoids an oversalted, soupy result.
Distractors assume linear scaling or that the pot alone determines seasoning.

items.prompt: A friend says, "Running my knife along a honing steel sharpens it, so I never need a stone." Which critique is most accurate?

options.label: A steel mainly works when used with oil, and dry passes tend to dull the blade further over time
Honing removes about as much metal as a stone does, but it suits thin, flexible blades best
Honing realigns a bent edge but removes little metal, so a dull edge needs a stone
Honing is enough for softer carbon steel blades, since stainless blades rarely bend at the edge

rubric: Honing straightens a rolled edge without removing much metal; real dullness requires grinding on a stone or similar.
Distractors blur honing with sharpening or invent material-specific rules.

items.prompt: Which statements about resting a thick roast after cooking are well supported? Select all that apply.

options.label: Larger roasts gain more carryover heat than thin steaks, so they need more allowance
Internal temperature keeps rising for several minutes, so pulling it slightly under target is reasonable
Resting lets juices redistribute, so less liquid runs out when the roast is carved
Resting reheats the surface, so the crust re-crisps as the roast sits
Wrapping the roast tightly in foil keeps the crust crisp while it rests

rubric: Carryover cooking, juice redistribution and mass-dependent heat gain are well established.
Tight foil traps steam and softens the crust; resting does not re-crisp it.

items.prompt: You reduced a pan sauce made with store-bought stock, and it now tastes too salty. Guests arrive in 10 minutes and you want to keep its body and flavor. Which fix is best?

options.label: Stir in sugar until the saltiness is masked, since sweetness cancels sodium in the sauce
Whisk in unsalted stock or water with a knob of butter, then brighten with a little lemon juice
Drop in a raw potato and simmer, since it absorbs the extra salt and leaves the sauce balanced
Keep simmering for several more minutes, since salt cooks off as the sauce thickens and reduces

rubric: Dilution lowers salt concentration; fat restores body and acid rebalances flavor.
Distractors rely on myths: potatoes absorb salt, sugar cancels it, or salt evaporates.

items.prompt: You need roast chicken pieces (45 min at 220C), potatoes (40 min), green beans (12 min) and a pan sauce from the roasting fond, all ready together from one oven. Which plan meets every constraint?

options.label: Make the sauce first in the roasting pan, then roast chicken and potatoes on top of it for 45 minutes
Roast the chicken alone, then cook the potatoes and beans afterward at the same temperature for 40 minutes
Roast chicken and potatoes together, add beans for the last 12 minutes, then make the sauce in the pan while the chicken rests
Roast everything including the beans from the start, then make the sauce in a clean pan from the juices

rubric: Staggering the beans fits the times, and the pan sauce needs fond that exists only after roasting.
Distractors overcook the beans, lack fond, or add serial time that breaks the finishing constraint.

items.prompt: A pancake recipe relies on baking soda and 1 cup of buttermilk. You have only plain milk and lemon juice. Which substitution meets the need for both liquid and acid?

options.label: Plain milk alone, since baking soda rises on heat and does not need acid to produce its gas
Plain milk with an extra half teaspoon of baking soda, to make up for the missing sourness
Plain milk with a tablespoon of lemon juice, rested about 5 minutes, so the acid can react with baking soda
Plain milk with a tablespoon of lemon juice added to the batter after the pancakes have been flipped

rubric: Baking soda needs an acid to react; soured milk supplies liquid and acidity in the right form.
Distractors add more base, mistime the acid, or assume soda works without acid.

items.prompt: Design a vinaigrette for bitter greens that stays emulsified for about two hours and is not harshly sharp. Which formula and method meets both constraints?

options.label: Three parts oil to one part vinegar with a teaspoon of mustard and pinch of honey, oil whisked in slowly
Three parts oil to one part vinegar, all poured in together without stirring, since time will blend them
Mostly water with a little oil and vinegar, since extra water thins the dressing and softens the sharpness
Equal parts oil and vinegar shaken once with salt, since a strong acid keeps the dressing from separating

rubric: A 3:1 ratio softens acidity, mustard is an emulsifier, and slow whisking disperses oil into stable droplets.
Distractors omit an emulsifier or technique, or use ratios that stay sharp or separate.

items.prompt: You have a weak home burner and must make a beef and broccoli stir-fry for four that browns rather than steams. Which plan meets that constraint?

options.label: Sear dry, evenly cut beef in small batches in a very hot pan, set it aside, then finish with vegetables and sauce
Put everything in the pan at once and cover it, so trapped steam cooks the beef and broccoli quickly and evenly
Simmer the broccoli and beef in the sauce first to cook them through, then brown them briefly at the end on medium heat
Marinate the beef in a thin sauce, then cook all of it in one crowded layer, letting the liquid reduce slowly over medium heat

rubric: Small batches of dry food keep the pan hot enough to brown, and recombining at the end preserves it.
Distractors add steam or excess liquid, which defeats browning on a weak burner.

items.prompt: A stovetop beef stew recipe must become hands-off and keep deep flavor in the oven. Which adaptation plan meets both constraints?

options.label: Sear the meat on the stove, add liquid halfway up, cover, and cook at about 150C until tender
Brown the meat and simmer it on the stove for an hour, then move the pot to a warm oven
Sear the meat, submerge it fully in cold stock, and leave the pot uncovered at 200C
Skip the sear and put the raw ingredients in a covered pot at 220C so everything cooks faster

rubric: Searing builds flavor, then covered low oven heat gives gentle even braising without attention.
Distractors skip browning, use heat that toughens meat, or keep the cook at the stove.

items.prompt: Design a food-safe plan for cooking a large pot of rice on Sunday to eat across the week. Which elements belong in a plan that meets food safety constraints? Select all that apply.

options.label: Refrigerate it promptly and keep it cold until it is reheated
Reheat the whole batch several times so any bacteria are killed each day
Reheat portions until steaming hot throughout, and only the amount needed
Spread the rice in shallow containers so it cools within about two hours
Leave the pot on the counter overnight to cool slowly and keep the grains fluffy

rubric: Fast cooling, cold storage and thorough single reheating limit bacterial growth and spore toxin formation.
Slow counter cooling and repeated reheating of the whole batch increase risk.

items.prompt: Marta wants a vegetarian lentil soup with deep flavor in 30 minutes, with no stock available. Her plan is to boil lentils, onion, carrot and water with salt, then serve. Which addition would best fix what this plan lacks?

options.label: Double the amount of water and boil longer so the vegetables release more flavor into the soup
Blend half the soup raw before cooking so the lentils release their flavor sooner into the liquid
Add all the salt at the start and boil hard so the seasoning has time to penetrate the lentils
Brown the onion and carrot in oil with tomato paste first, and finish with a splash of vinegar

rubric: Browning aromatics and tomato paste builds savory depth without stock, and acid at the end brightens flavor.
Distractors rely on dilution, salt timing or blending, none of which create depth.
